newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shilling plunges on renewed jitters.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shilling plunges on renewed jitters.

text.p: The Kenyan shilling slid further against the dollar on Wednesday on renewed pressure triggered by last week's cancellation of a key aid package by the IMF, commercial dealers said.
The shilling slipped to a commercial average of 67 against the dollar compared to 64.25 at close on Tuesday -- a decline of 4.28 percent, commercial dealers told Reuters.

The latest losses meant the shilling has depreciated by a total of 12.6 percent since news on Friday that the IMF had halted a three-year Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) to Kenya in a row over corruption.

Commercial dealers said investors were seriously alarmed at President Daniel arap Moi's comments that Kenyans would have to become self-reliant and that the IMF package was insignificant compared to Kenya's total economic requirements.

"Things are very bad. The market is very nervous," said a dealer, adding that the amount of hard currencies on the market was very little and every dealer sought to cover whatever positions they held.
But commercial dealers said the shilling came under renewed pressure on Tuesday because of a shortfall in expected inflows from the coffee and tea sectors -- Kenya's main commodity exports.
Another dealer said: "This is the first time the market has reacted to such news. It's actually moving an average of a shilling a day since the IMF announcement."
There were bids as low as 69 on Wednesday morning. The shilling's lowest level stands at around 69.22 in October 1993.
"If the central bank does not come in, a rate of 70 will be touched very soon," one dealer said.
On Tuesday Moi downplayed the IMF ruling and told a rally in the tea and coffee growing central Kenya that the IMF loan amounted to $205 million when Kenya's was a $3 billion economy.
Moi said Kenya would improve tax collection and commodity exports to meet any shortfalls arising from the IMF decision.
But commercial dealers said exporters were also refusing to sell their dollars, increasing pressure on the besieged shilling.

On Monday, Moi's cabinet urged investors to remain calm, saying Kenyan citizens should build the economy from their own meagre resources. But Kenyan executives and industrial analysts rejected as nonsense the cabinet statement.
"That's nonsense. Kenya cannot survive without (Western) aid," a leading Nairobi-based investment analyst said.
A high-ranking corporate executive also said the country should brace itself for tougher times to come.

The shilling losses were expected to increase pressure on the 73-year old president, who is facing a go-slow by air traffic controllers and a national strike on Friday planned by an opposition-backed alliance pressing for political reforms.

Moi and his ruling KANU party are widely expected to extend a 19-year regime in elections that must be held by the end of this year. They face an opposition that has found a fragile cohesion in demands for constitutional reforms.
